title: Electric Charge and Fields
description: The invisible force that holds atoms together and powers civilisation

concepts.title: Electric Charge and Coulomb's Law
concepts.contentHtml:
Electric charge comes in two types: positive and negative. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract. Charge is quantised — all charges are multiples of the elementary charge e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (the charge of a proton).

Coulomb's Law gives the force between two point charges: F = kq₁q₂/r². Like gravity, it's an inverse-square law — double the distance, quarter the force. But electricity can be both attractive and repulsive, and it's enormously stronger than gravity at atomic scales.

concepts.title: Electric Fields
concepts.contentHtml:
Rather than thinking of charges acting on each other at a distance, we say charges create an electric field in the space around them. Other charges then feel a force from the field at their location.

Electric field strength E = F/q — the force per unit positive test charge. Field lines point away from positive charges, toward negative charges. Where they're dense, the field is strong.

This field concept, introduced by Faraday, was revolutionary: it made electromagnetism a local theory. A charge responds to the field right where it is, not to distant sources directly.

concepts.title: Electric Potential and Voltage
concepts.contentHtml:
Electric potential (V) at a point is the potential energy per unit charge. Moving a charge through a potential difference does work.

Voltage is the potential difference between two points. A 9 V battery means each coulomb of charge gains 9 J of energy moving from negative to positive terminal.

The relationship between field and potential: E = −dV/dx (field points in the direction of decreasing potential). Equipotential lines are always perpendicular to field lines — like contour lines on a map relative to the steepest slope direction.

title: Magnetism and Electrodynamics
description: Moving charges create magnetic fields — and magnetic fields move charges

concepts.title: Magnetic Fields and Forces
concepts.contentHtml:
Magnetic fields exert forces on moving charges: F = qv × B. The force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the field — a cross product. This is why charged particles in magnetic fields spiral in circles rather than accelerating in a straight line.

Magnetic field lines form closed loops — there are no magnetic monopoles (isolated north or south poles). The SI unit of magnetic field is the tesla (T). Earth's field is about 50 μT; MRI machines use 1.5–7 T.

concepts.title: Faraday's Law — Electromagnetic Induction
concepts.contentHtml:
Michael Faraday's 1831 discovery: a changing magnetic flux through a loop induces an electromotive force (voltage) in the loop. This is the principle behind electric generators, transformers, and induction cooktops.

The induced EMF = −dΦ/dt, where Φ = B·A is the magnetic flux. The minus sign (Lenz's law) means the induced current opposes the change that caused it — nature resists change.

Faraday had little mathematical training, but his physical intuition led Maxwell to the full mathematical theory. Generators work by rotating a coil in a magnetic field, continuously changing the flux.

concepts.title: Ampere's Law and Current-Carrying Wires
concepts.contentHtml:
A current-carrying wire creates a magnetic field circling around it — first discovered by Oersted in 1820 (he noticed a compass needle deflect when a circuit was switched on).

Ampere's Law: the line integral of B around any closed loop equals μ₀ times the enclosed current. For a long straight wire: B = μ₀I/(2πr) — field falls off with distance from the wire.

Two parallel wires carrying current in the same direction attract each other; opposite currents repel. This is how the ampere (unit of current) was historically defined — by the force between parallel wires.

title: Maxwell's Equations
description: Four elegant equations that unify all of classical electromagnetism

concepts.title: The Four Equations
concepts.contentHtml:
James Clerk Maxwell (1865) unified electricity, magnetism, and light in four equations:

1. Gauss's Law (E): Electric field lines diverge from charges — ∇·E = ρ/ε₀.
2. Gauss's Law (B): No magnetic monopoles — ∇·B = 0.
3. Faraday's Law: Changing B creates E — ∇×E = −∂B/∂t.
4. Ampere-Maxwell Law: Currents AND changing E create B — ∇×B = μ₀J + μ₀ε₀∂E/∂t.

Maxwell's key addition was the displacement current (μ₀ε₀∂E/∂t) in equation 4 — without it the equations were inconsistent, and electromagnetic waves could not exist.

concepts.title: Electromagnetic Waves
concepts.contentHtml:
From Maxwell's equations, a changing electric field creates a magnetic field and vice versa. This self-sustaining interplay produces electromagnetic waves — oscillating E and B fields propagating through space.

The wave equation derived from Maxwell's equations gives a speed: c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀). Plugging in the constants: c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s — exactly the measured speed of light. Maxwell concluded light is an electromagnetic wave.

This was one of the great unifications in physics history: electricity, magnetism, and optics — once thought separate — are all aspects of one phenomenon.

concepts.title: Gauss's Laws and Symmetry
concepts.contentHtml:
Gauss's Law for electric fields (∇·E = ρ/ε₀) is a local statement of Coulomb's Law: charge is the source of electric field lines. The integral form — the total electric flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀ — lets us easily compute fields for symmetric charge distributions.

Gauss's Law for magnetism (∇·B = 0) states that magnetic field lines have no sources or sinks — they form closed loops. This rules out magnetic monopoles. If monopoles existed, ∇·B = ρ_m/μ₀ instead.

Both Gauss laws follow from the symmetry of their respective fields under the divergence theorem.

title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum and Light
description: Radio waves to gamma rays — one phenomenon, many faces

concepts.title: The Spectrum
concepts.contentHtml:
All electromagnetic waves travel at c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum and are characterised by frequency f and wavelength λ: c = fλ.

In order of increasing frequency (decreasing wavelength): radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays. These are not fundamentally different things — only the frequency differs.

Visible light (400–700 nm) is a tiny sliver. Radio waves can be kilometres long. Gamma rays have wavelengths smaller than an atomic nucleus. The energy of a photon E = hf, so higher frequency means more energetic photons.

concepts.title: Polarisation and Interference
concepts.contentHtml:
EM waves are transverse — E and B oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel. Polarisation describes the orientation of the E field. Sunlight is unpolarised (all orientations); polarising filters transmit only one orientation. This is why polarised sunglasses reduce glare from horizontal surfaces.

Interference occurs when two waves overlap. Young's double-slit experiment (1801) showed light interferes — alternating bright and dark bands. This proved light is a wave, not just a stream of particles. (Quantum mechanics later showed it's both.)

concepts.title: Applications: Radio, Lasers, and Wi-Fi
concepts.contentHtml:
Maxwell's equations underpin virtually all modern technology:

Radio/TV: oscillating electrons in an antenna emit EM waves; receiving antenna electrons are set oscillating by the incoming wave — Faraday induction in action.

Lasers: stimulated emission produces coherent, monochromatic light — all photons in phase. Used in surgery, fibre-optic communications, barcode scanners, and LiDAR.

Wi-Fi/5G: microwave and millimetre-wave EM radiation encodes data. The physics is pure Maxwell; engineering is everything else.

Every wireless signal ever sent has obeyed Maxwell's equations.

title: Quantum Electrodynamics and Frontier EM
description: How quantum mechanics and electromagnetism merge into QED

concepts.title: Quantum Electrodynamics (QED)
concepts.contentHtml:
Classical electromagnetism is a field theory — E and B are continuous fields filling space. But at quantum scales, the electromagnetic field is quantised: it comes in discrete packets called photons.

QED, developed by Feynman, Schwinger, and Tomonaga (Nobel 1965), describes how charged particles interact by exchanging virtual photons. It is the most precisely tested theory in science: the electron's magnetic moment predicted by QED matches experiment to 12 significant figures.

In QED, light and matter are no longer separate — they are excitations of interacting quantum fields.

concepts.title: Electromagnetic Duality and Monopoles
concepts.contentHtml:
Maxwell's equations in vacuum are almost perfectly symmetric between E and B. If you swap E → cB and cB → −E (a duality transformation), equations 1 and 2 swap and equations 3 and 4 swap. The asymmetry — ∇·E = ρ/ε₀ but ∇·B = 0 — comes from the absence of magnetic monopoles.

Paul Dirac showed in 1931 that if even one magnetic monopole existed anywhere in the universe, it would explain why electric charge is quantised. Grand unified theories predict monopoles were produced in the Big Bang, but none have ever been detected.

concepts.title: Special Relativity and EM Unification
concepts.contentHtml:
Maxwell's equations were already relativistically correct before special relativity was invented. Einstein's 1905 paper was partly motivated by a puzzle: a magnet moving toward a coil and a coil moving toward a magnet produce the same current — but classical theory gave two different explanations. Relativity unified them: E and B are components of a single electromagnetic field tensor, mixed by Lorentz boosts.

A pure electric field in one reference frame appears as a mix of electric and magnetic fields in a moving frame. Magnetism is a relativistic effect of electricity. The force between two parallel wires can be derived entirely from Coulomb's Law plus special relativity.

concepts.title: Gauss's Laws
concepts.contentHtml:
The first two of Maxwell's four equations are Gauss's laws:

∇·E = ρ/ε₀ — electric flux out of any closed surface equals enclosed charge over ε₀.
∇·B = 0 — no magnetic monopoles; whatever B-field flux enters a surface also exits.

Gauss's law for E gives Coulomb's inverse-square law as a special case for a point charge. The B-field version is symmetric in form but profoundly different in content — it says magnetism has no isolated 'sources'.

concepts.title: Faraday's Law
concepts.contentHtml:
∇×E = -∂B/∂t. A changing magnetic field creates a curling electric field.

This is the law of induction — wave a magnet near a coil and current flows. Generators, transformers, electric guitars all run on Faraday's law.

The minus sign (Lenz's law) is critical: induced currents oppose the change that produced them. This is energy conservation in disguise — induced EMF can never run a perpetual motion machine.

concepts.title: Ampère-Maxwell Law
concepts.contentHtml:
∇×B = μ₀J + μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t. A magnetic curl arises from currents (J) and from changing electric fields.

Ampère originally wrote only the J term. Maxwell added the displacement current term ε₀ ∂E/∂t — without which his equations would have been inconsistent for time-varying fields.

That extra term enabled electromagnetic waves: a changing E creates B, a changing B creates E, and the two waves bootstrap each other through space at speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀). Maxwell calculated c and noticed it matched the measured speed of light. Light is electromagnetism.

title: EM in Materials
description: What happens when fields meet matter

concepts.title: Polarization & Dielectrics
concepts.contentHtml:
Insert an insulator into an electric field. The molecules' positive and negative charges shift slightly relative to each other — the material gains polarization P.

P points along the applied field, and the resulting bound surface charges set up a field that opposes it, weakening the field inside. The result: the field inside is reduced by a factor of the dielectric constant κ. Capacitors with dielectrics store more charge at a given voltage.

Permittivity ε = ε₀ κ characterizes the material. Water has κ ≈ 80; air ≈ 1; vacuum exactly 1.

concepts.title: Magnetism in Materials
concepts.contentHtml:
Materials respond to magnetic fields in three main ways. Diamagnetic materials weakly oppose the applied field (water, copper). Paramagnetic materials weakly enhance it (aluminum, oxygen). Ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt) align with it strongly and retain magnetization after the field is removed.

Ferromagnetism is a quantum phenomenon involving the exchange interaction. Below the Curie temperature, electron spins align spontaneously into domains, giving iron its enormous magnetic permeability.

concepts.title: Conductors and Optics of Solids
concepts.contentHtml:
In a conductor, free electrons rearrange to cancel any applied static E-field — the field inside a conductor is zero. That's why a Faraday cage works.

At optical frequencies, the electrons can't keep up with rapid oscillations. Instead, they oscillate with the field, absorbing some, reflecting some. The result: shiny metals (good reflectors), colored gems (selective absorption), transparent insulators.

The full story uses the dielectric function ε(ω), which encodes how a material's response varies with frequency. Plasma frequency is the cutoff above which metals become transparent (ultraviolet for most metals).

title: Antennas, Radiation, & Modern EM
description: How EM waves are made, sent, and used

concepts.title: Why Accelerated Charges Radiate
concepts.contentHtml:
A charge moving at constant velocity carries fields with it but does not radiate. Acceleration is what creates radiating EM waves.

The Larmor formula gives the power radiated: P = q²a²/(6πε₀c³). Since a appears squared, even small accelerations of large charges (or any acceleration of relativistic particles) can radiate enormously.

This is why radio antennas are oscillators (charges accelerating back and forth) and why electron synchrotrons emit x-rays (charges in circular motion).

concepts.title: Antennas
concepts.contentHtml:
An antenna couples electric circuits to free-space EM waves. The simplest is a half-wave dipole — its length matches half the wavelength of the desired frequency.

FM radio at 100 MHz has a wavelength of 3 m, so antennas are about 1.5 m. WiFi at 2.4 GHz: 12 cm wavelength, antennas a few cm. Wi-Fi at 5 GHz and 5G millimetre-wave bands (24+ GHz): tiny antennas, but engineering gets fierce as wavelengths shrink.

Phased arrays (multiple coordinated antennas) can steer beams electronically without moving parts — used in modern radar and 5G.

concepts.title: Modern Applications
concepts.contentHtml:
EM theory is tested every day in technology: GPS satellites broadcast precisely timed microwaves; MRI flips proton spins with radio pulses and reads back the relaxation; CMB measurements probe the universe at 160 GHz.

Wireless power transfer uses inductive (close range) or resonant (medium range) coupling. Metamaterials engineer effective permittivities and permeabilities far beyond natural values, enabling cloaking demonstrations and superlenses.

The same equations Maxwell wrote in the 1860s drive every smartphone, every radar, every fiber-optic cable. They've held up for 160 years and counting.
